title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
short: Parallel capacitances add, and series capacitances combine by reciprocals, the opposite of resistors.
trouble: Students add series capacitances directly, as they would series resistors.

blocks.html: Circuits often combine several capacitors. The rules look like the ones for resistors, but switched: the series rule for capacitors is the parallel rule for resistors, and the other way around.

In parallel, each capacitor has the same voltage and their charges add: $Q = C_1V + C_2V$, so $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2$. It is like making the plates bigger. In series, the inner plates are connected only to each other, so the charge they hold is pulled across from one to the other: every capacitor carries the same charge $Q$. Their voltages add: $V = \dfrac{Q}{C_1} + \dfrac{Q}{C_2}$, so $\dfrac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2}$. It is like making the gap wider.

Parallel: $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots$ (same $V$, charges add). Series: $\dfrac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \cdots$ (same $Q$, voltages add), smaller than any one of them.

blocks.title: A combination
blocks.q: A $6\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is in series with a parallel pair of $2\,\mu\text{F}$ and $4\,\mu\text{F}$. Find $C_{\text{eq}}$.

blocks.html: Adding series capacitances directly, as you would series resistors. Putting capacitors in series is like widening the gap, which lowers capacitance. Check: a series combination is always smaller than its smallest capacitor, and a parallel one bigger than its biggest.

In series, the smaller capacitor ends up with the larger voltage, because both hold the same charge and $V = Q/C$. That is the opposite of series resistors, where the larger resistor takes the larger voltage.
